transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes (recording)
Attendees (Redwood): Samir Gupta, Leah Park, Diego Ramos
Attendees (Customer): Maria Lopez (CTO), Darren Cole (Lead ML Engineer), Priya Nair (Infra Architect), Ethan Wu (SRE)
Links referenced: hybrid-routing deck (https://app.redwood.ai/decks/hybrid-routing.pdf), benchmark spreadsheet (private link shared post-call)

Agenda (as stated):
- Quick context and production constraints (Nexa)
- Dedicated vs hosted routing for steady-state throughput
- KV cache eviction strategies and prefix caching implications
- Batching, quantization tradeoffs and observed tail latency
- VPC/on-prem connectivity and security items for pilot
- Recap + next steps

[00:00:12] Samir: Hey Maria, thanks for making time — can you kick us off with a quick context on what you need?

[00:00:22] Maria: Yeah hi, Samir. So our main driver is we need consistent 99th percentile latency under 220ms for our real-time credit decisions, and cost matters because we run millions of requests a day. We're currently on a mix — some hosted endpoints with VendorX and an internal GKE-based rapid inference cluster for high-value accounts. The gaps are noisy neighbor spikes and unpredictable tail latency.

[00:00:51] Samir: Got it. Leah will dive into runtime/kv specifics, I want to understand the SLOs — 220ms p99, is p50 target too?

[00:00:59] Maria: p50 around 40–60ms. Also encryption-in-transit and KMS for model inputs is non-negotiable.

[00:01:12] Leah: Great. Quick clarifying question — Darren, what's your typical sequence length and top model families you test?

[00:01:20] Darren: Most prompts are short — 18 to 64 tokens average. For some enrichment flows we go up to 250 but rare. We're testing both open models (Llama variants) and a tuned transformer we call "Nexa-Tune" that is ~7B.

[00:01:36] Leah: Cool. That matters for batching and kv cache behavior — small sequences favor aggressive batching but we need to ensure latency headroom.

[00:01:45] [00:02:02] Diego: Quick note, sometimes Fireflies timestamps jump, ignore the double stamp — sorry.

[00:02:10] Priya: Also a security note: we need audit logs and per-request key tagging for KMS. Can Redwood's private route sign requests with our key?

[00:02:22] Samir: Yes, in Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit logs. For hosted we offer envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys but can integrate customer KMS via our dedicated plan. We'll include the exact compliance matrix.

[00:02:40] Leah: Ok, moving onto runtime design. There are three routing patterns we discussed last week: 1) Pure hosted multi-tenant default, 2) Dedicated pool for predictable throughput, and 3) Hybrid routing — dynamically route by policy (latency-sensitive -> dedicated, best-effort -> hosted). Today we focused on the hybrid story and how KV cache eviction impacts tail latency.

[00:03:10] [00:03:27] Darren: On KV cache, our current internal inference caches often evict aggressively since we have lots of short-lived prefixes. We saw p99 spikes when the KV cache misses and have to repopulate the cache, generating many small KV fetches.

[00:03:40] Leah: Right — two common causes: small LRU caches with high churn, and cache lookups that aren't coalesced with batching. Redwood runtime tries to do prefix coalescing and a background prefetch for hot keys, but that can be tuned.

[00:03:59] Maria: Can you explain "prefix coalescing" again? Our infra team misheard it as "prefix colising" last call.

[00:04:07] Leah: (laughs) Sure — prefix coalescing groups requests that share the same KV prefix so the runtime can do one KV lookup and share the result. If you have many similar prompts with the same initial tokens, we can avoid repeated KV fetches. But it needs a predictable prompt shape and request tagging.

[00:04:28] Darren: Our prompts vary a lot — personalization tokens at end. How do you handle variable suffixes?

[00:04:33] Leah: We support multiple keying strategies: full prompt keys, prefix-only keys, and segmented keys (prefix + user bucket). Your team can pick — prefix-only reduces misses but risks staleness for personalized content.

[00:04:48] Ethan: Any mis-transcription — I think you said "KV cash" earlier — haha.

[00:04:53] (laughter)

[00:04:57] Leah: Noted. Regarding eviction policies, we recommend a multi-tier approach: LRU at the GPU node, plus a global hot-set tracker that keeps the top N keys in memory across the pool. For hybrid routing, the dedicated pool keeps a pinned hot-set to ensure predictable p99. Hosted side has a smaller hot-set and higher miss rates.

[00:05:25] Maria: What's the memory footprint? Our GPUs are A10s in the cloud right now; we can't blow past 32GB for cache.

[00:05:33] Leah: For a 7B model, a moderate per-node cache for top 1M tokens can be ~8–12GB depending on kv representation and compression. With quantized keys and compressed vectors it's smaller. We'll run a memory estimate with your trace.

[00:05:49] Samir: Let's switch to batching and quantization tradeoffs — Leah, can you summarize observed latencies for INT8 quant vs FP16 at different batch sizes?

[00:05:59] Leah: Sure — in our bench on 7B models: FP16 at batch=1 median latency ~45ms, p99 ~220ms depending on KV misses. INT8 quant (server-friendly kernels) reduces median to ~30ms but can increase variance a little on certain kernels — i.e., p99 sometimes moves to ~260ms if you hit a slower GEMM path. However, INT8 reduces memory and allows higher effective concurrency meaning fewer queuing delays. The trade is occasional output quality regressions; we measured a small BLEU/QA delta.

[00:06:34] Darren: How do you surface the quality delta? We need deterministic evals for compliance.

[00:06:38] Leah: We attach per-prompt eval hooks — Redwood Optimize can run your prompt set across configurations and give a quality delta matrix. We can instrument diffs and flag prompts that degrade beyond a threshold.

[00:06:52] Priya: If dedicated is pinned, can we force FP16 there but allow hosted to use INT8 for best-effort?

[00:06:59] Samir: Yes, that's a typical policy — dedicated for high-value traffic with stricter model/quantization policy, hosted for cost-optimized inference. Our routing can do per-route model/quantization binding.

[00:07:12] [00:07:35] Maria: On the dedicated pool guarantees — what does predictable throughput mean? We need a SLA-ish number for p99 under nominal load.

[00:07:43] Diego: We size pool capacity to meet your committed RPS with headroom; for the pilot we'll propose capacity and measured p99 under synthetic replay. The Dedicated contract includes throughput reservation and a latency target for the commit. If you need hard real-time (e.g., sub-150ms p99) we can do a custom sizing and nerve center to provide additional overprovision.

[00:08:03] Ethan: And noisy neighbor isolation — how do you prevent other tenants on the same hardware causing stalls?

[00:08:09] Leah: Two levers: 1) Dedicated tenancy (no other customers on that pool), 2) Within a multi-tenant host we do per-tenant CUDA context isolation + GPU memory and clock gating where supported; but the strongest isolation is dedicated pools. For shared pools we have throttling and graceful shedding by routing and fallback.

[00:08:28] Priya: Our compliance team prefers dedicated if possible. Cost is the constraint. Can hybrid routing move traffic to hosted when dedicated is saturated?

[00:08:36] Samir: Yes — policy-based fallback: route to hosted model variants with quantization/caching tuned for cost, and mark the request with "best-effort" tag. We recommend progressive fallback: first route to a cheaper quant variant on dedicated, then hosted.

[00:08:51] [00:09:07] Darren: What about KV replication between hosted and dedicated? If a KV hit exists on hosted, can dedicated reuse it or vice versa?

[00:09:14] Leah: We avoid cross-tenant shared KV in hosted. For hybrid you can enable a shared hot-set replication via a secure bridge — but it's an explicit config. Replication adds consistency and network overhead; usually we replicate hot keys (top 100k) asynchronously to reduce p99. For strict privacy you can keep them isolated.

[00:09:37] Maria: That makes sense. For Nexa, data residency matters — that replication needs to keep keys in-region.

[00:09:43] Samir: We can pin replication traffic to region and only use customer VPC peering.

[00:09:50] Leah: Moving to batching: Redwood supports continuous batching and dynamic batch sizing with tail-aware cutoff. For short prompts, a small micro-batch window (5–8ms) yields big throughput gains without huge latency cost; but that window must be tuned to p99 SLOs.

[00:10:05] Darren: Is there jitter introduced by dynamic batching? We saw jitter in our GKE runner when bursty traffic hit and batching ramped up.

[00:10:12] Leah: Yes jitter happens — our runtime uses a tail-aware timeout that reduces batching when p99 starts rising. We also provide backpressure tokens to upstream services. The key is workload characterization — your trace will help pick the right timeouts.

[00:10:27] Ethan: On the security front, does Redwood's hosted product support token-level logging with redaction rules?

[00:10:34] Samir: Hosted does support per-token cost/latency logs; for PII we provide built-in redaction and customer-configured patterns. Private offers full event logs that you can ship to Splunk/Datadog.

[00:10:46] Priya: Any special network requirements for the pilot? We prefer VPC peering with a restricted endpoint and egress rules — no public internet for model traffic.

[00:10:54] Samir: For Dedicated/Private we support VPC peering, internal endpoints, and optional on-prem packages for air-gapped installs. We'll include the network diagram in the deck.

[00:11:03] [00:11:20] Leah: Back to quantization: practical tip — stick with per-channel quant for weights and FP16 for activations if you care about determinism. INT8 math can be non-deterministic across different kernel paths. Also, quantization-aware finetune helps minimize quality drift.

[00:11:38] Darren: We could finetune a quant-aware version if it keeps quality within our guardrails. Would Redwood help with that workflow?

[00:11:44] Samir: Yes, Redwood Optimize and our Research partners can run quant-aware fine-tuning pipelines and evals as part of the onboarding. It's an add-on but we can run an initial eval for pilot.

[00:11:56] Maria: There was a line in earlier notes about "kernel selection" — can you explain how that impacts latency spikes?

[00:12:03] Leah: The runtime chooses different GEMM kernels depending on model shape and sequence length; some kernels perform well on median but have pathological p99 for certain sequence lengths. Kernel choice is a compound of hardware, model block size, and quant path. We run kernel selection benchmarking and pin the kernel family for dedicated deployments to avoid runtime jitters.

[00:12:22] Diego: That's why the dedicated pool is useful — you can pin a kernel and quantization config across the fleet and keep behavior stable.

[00:12:30] [00:12:46] Ethan: About observability: can we get token-by-token latency breakdown exported? Our SRE wants to see NVLink copy time vs kernel exec.

[00:12:54] Leah: Yes, Redwood Console exports per-request token timing, broken into network, KV lookup, batching wait, kernel exec. For private deployments we can stream raw traces to your tracing backend.

[00:13:08] Darren: We need regression alerts when p95/p99 increases by more than 15% — can Redwood tie that to automatic rollback?

[00:13:13] Samir: Yes, rollouts in Redwood include automatic fallback: if latency or quality regressions exceed thresholds on canary we automatically revert to last known good model/variant.

[00:13:24] Maria: Good. A few quick questions I want explicit answers to in the follow-up doc: 1) memory estimate for pinned hot-set on A10s, 2) expected p99 under pilot sizing (synthetic replay), 3) network diagram for VPC peering, 4) quant vs FP16 quality delta for our 500-sample prompts.

[00:13:44] Samir: We'll deliver those items. Leah will run the bench and Diego will send the network diagram.

[00:13:51] [00:14:10] Leah: Quick note on cost math: often teams think INT8 always saves X%; the reality is it's context-sensitive. You gain compute efficiency, but if you need extra evaluation and fine-tuning overhead, it can reduce net savings. We'll model both direct per-token compute cost and operational overhead in the spreadsheet.

[00:14:27] Darren: What about failover behavior? If dedicated pool loses nodes, do requests queue or fall back?

[00:14:34] Leah: We do progressive fallback: queue with backpressure up to a threshold (configurable), then route to a fallback host (hosted variant). We also support warm standby pods to reduce cold-start.

[00:14:45] Ethan: Any special considerations for on-prem? We have some customers requiring on-prem inference for the highest-security flows.

[00:14:52] Samir: On-prem package is available — we ship the runtime and orchestration agents. On-prem customers run the control plane in a private VPC or offline. On-prem deploys can integrate with your KMS/HSM and local logging.

[00:15:04] [00:15:20] Maria: Ok, can you outline a pilot plan briefly now?

[00:15:25] Samir: Pilot plan (high level): 1) Week 0: collect traces and prompts (Nexa to send), 2) Week 1: Redwood runs replay on a dedicated pilot pool and experiments with caching strategies + quant variants, 3) Week 2: run a short production-slice with real traffic routed 10% to dedicated pool, measure p50/p95/p99 and quality, 4) Decision point and follow-up contract.

[00:15:48] Priya: For the replay, what's the expected data we need to send? An hour of anonymized request/response pairs?

[00:15:56] Leah: Yes — 1 hour of representative traffic plus a 500-prompt evaluation set covers most bench needs. Mask PII and use tokenized dumps or a gzipped NDJSON.

[00:16:07] Maria: We'll get that to you by Thursday.

[00:16:12] [00:16:30] Darren: One more technical nit: is there a way to pin users to the same GPU node to improve cache locality? We have heavy users with repeated prefixes.

[00:16:37] Leah: We support session affinity by user-bucket. For high-value accounts we can ensure requests hit the same node (sticky routing) so local KV cache hits improve. Tradeoff is uneven load distribution.

[00:16:51] Diego: We typically use sticky routing only for the top X% of traffic. For the rest, global routing keeps utilization balanced.

[00:16:59] [00:17:20] Ethan: Anything about SRE on-call integrations? PagerDuty?

[00:17:25] Samir: Alerts can be exported to PagerDuty/Slack and include traces. Diego will include an example alerting config in the follow-up.

[00:17:34] Maria: Great. I'm getting a lot from this call. A quick question about dataset drift detection tied to quantization regressions — can Optimize run continuous checks?

[00:17:42] Leah: Yes, Redwood Optimize can run scheduled evals and trigger alerts if quality drifts beyond thresholds. We can also retain historical evals to debug regressions.

[00:17:52] Darren: If we want to try quantized finetune, what's the timeline?

[00:17:56] Samir: Initial quant-aware finetune and evaluation typical 1–2 weeks depending on dataset size. We can scope it into the pilot if you want.

[00:18:04] [00:18:22] Maria: Ok — let's do the pilot with a small quant-aware finetune experiment included. Cost estimate? Samir, ballpark?

[00:18:29] Samir: Ballpark for a 2-week dedicated pilot with a small finetune: mid-five-figure USD, depends on committed RPS and model choices. We'll put precise numbers in the spreadsheet.

[00:18:41] Priya: I have to check procurement thresholds. We may need a PO.

[00:18:45] Samir: Understood — we'll send a pilot agreement template.

[00:18:52] [00:19:10] (brief side conversation — audio noise, muffled — transcription imperfect)

[00:19:30] Leah: Quick technical aside — KV eviction can be improved with tiered storage: keep very hot keys in GPU DRAM, warm keys in host RAM, cold keys on remote redis. For p99-sensitive flows keep the hot-set small and pinned.

[00:19:53] Darren: Would that add operational complexity?

[00:19:56] Leah: Some, yes. But Redwood can manage the tiering as part of Dedicated.

[00:20:04] Maria: Any risk of cross-tenant leaks with tiered remote caches?

[00:20:09] Leah: We never share tenant namespaces; remote caches are namespaced and optionally encrypted in transit and at rest.

[00:20:18] [00:20:34] Diego: We're approaching the networking questions. Priya, do you want us to present a sample VPC peering diagram in the follow-up or a fully detailed one?

[00:20:41] Priya: Detailed with CIDR ranges and firewall rules we can hand to networking. Also need KMS policy example.

[00:20:48] Diego: We'll include both.

[00:20:55] Maria: Ok, let's do a quick recap and final clarifying questions.

[00:21:05] Samir: Recap: 1) Pilot: 2-week dedicated pool with 10% live traffic slice in Week 2; 2) Bench: Redwood team runs KV eviction + quantization matrix on Nexa traces; 3) Security: include VPC peering + KMS integration details; 4) Observability: console dashboards + token timings; 5) Next steps: deck, spreadsheet, and pilot contract shared by 2025-11-20.

[00:21:32] Maria: That works. One last nit — can you add an example of an automatic rollback policy in the doc?

[00:21:39] Samir: Yes — we'll include a sample policy.

[00:21:44] Darren: Also please include samples of the eval diffs so our compliance team can see the exact prompt/response changes.

[00:21:50] Leah: We'll attach a diffs CSV and a small HTML render.

[00:21:56] Maria: Ok thanks everyone.

[00:22:03] Samir: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[00:22:10] (call winds down, small chatter about calendar invites)

End of recording.
